newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU may lower interest rates if all behave - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: EMU may lower interest rates if all behave - Waigel.

text.p: European economic and monetary union (EMU) could mean lower interest rates for all involved, but that pleasant prospect could be ruined by a single reckless member, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday.

Waigel said that in the time remaining until the scheduled January 1999 start of EMU, Germany would stress implementation of the stability pact agreed at the Dublin summit in December after arduous negotiations.
The pact, whose main backer is Germany, is designed to ensure that participating countries continue to exercise strict fiscal discipline even after the start of EMU.

"The creation of a larger and more productive European financial market offers an opportunity for falling market interest rates," Waigel said in an address prepared for delivery to the European Parliament.

But "uninhibited deficit spending by a single member state could drive interest rates to the heights for all. Stability- oriented fiscal policies by all participants are essential for the success of monetary union," he said.
The stability pact is an attempt to set rules that will prevent a single irresponsible state from causing problems for others, he said.

The start of the single European currency will create an economic zone large enough to represent a true alternative to the dollar, loosening Europe's links to the dollar's value and U.S. interest rates, he said.
"Europe will be able to orient itself more strongly on its own needs," he said.
Waigel said EMU was likely to start with far fewer participants than the 15 members of the European Union.

"In particular those (EU) members whose convergence efforts are not yet far enough along will need the additional degree of freedom offered by the fact that their exchange rates will remain flexible relative to the euro," he said.
Bonn itself is coming precariously close to missing the EMU deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product this year, the key year for deciding the starting line-up of EMU participants.

Over the weekend, Germany revised upward its forecast of its 1997 deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP from 2.5 percent earlier. But officials said it would remain strict in its interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty.

State secretary for finance Juergen Stark said in an interview with the Handelsblatt newspaper on Monday, "We will not be using the leeway that the treaty allows for interpreting the (convergence) criteria."

Waigel said to secure the success of EMU in the face of high unemployment, Germany and other countries must work to resolve the structural problems of the jobs market, as economic growth alone will remain too sluggish to create jobs.
High unemployment undermines efforts to meet the strict debt and deficit targets for EMU, by reducing tax revenues and increasing outlays for unemployment benefits.
Once EMU is implemented, participating countries will no longer be able to make use of foreign exchange adjustments as a buffer for their labour policies, Waigel said.
"The experiences of the past have clearly shown that low deficits are the basis for low interest rates, more investment, more growth and more jobs," Waigel said.
